title: What's the deal with accents?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore accents and how they differ from dialects, starting with a discussion of regional American accents and a New York Times dialect quiz. They cover how accents form in infancy (babies recognizing accents in the womb, the Japanese L/R perceptual pruning study by Patricia Kuhl, and the bear experiment), how bilingualism and language transfer affect second-language accents, and how English accents spread from Britain to Australia, the US and elsewhere. They discuss rhotic vs non-rhotic speech, the history of r-full and r-less accents in America, received pronunciation and the BBC, and the mid-Atlantic movie accent. They also cover accent perception and bias, British accents as movie villain shorthand, pop music singers' accents, UK grime, and UK accent discrimination. Listener mail from Nick in Indiana closes the episode about imagining the hosts' voices wrongly.
topics: babies recognize accents in the womb

segments.title: Opening banter and love of accents
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about how much they enjoy accents, Chuck's childhood Southern accent, and friends' regional speech. They note everyone has an accent even if they can't hear their own.

segments.title: Accent vs dialect and the NYT dialect quiz
segments.summary: They distinguish accent (how speech sounds) from dialect (vocabulary, slang, grammar), and discuss the New York Times dialect quiz and regional terms like median, kitty corner, and the devil beating his wife.

segments.title: Native vs second-language accents
segments.summary: Linguists split accents into native-language accents and foreign-language accents. Josh describes German class and his ability to mimic sounds, while noting others could not.

segments.title: Infant accent development and babies in the womb
segments.summary: Babies reportedly prefer the accent heard in the womb. Patricia Kuhl's work describes a language map pruned by exposure, and the Japanese L/R experiment with babies and a dancing bear shows how sound perception narrows by age one.
topics: babies recognize accents in the womb

segments.title: Bilingual children and language transfer
segments.summary: Children learn languages more easily when young, and bilingual households give kids multiple language maps. Language transfer can help or hinder second-language learning, as with German speakers and English th, Italians learning Spanish, and English speakers and Spanish P/B sounds.

segments.title: Learning an accent and the Munich beer garden story
segments.summary: Accents can be retrained with lots of listening and practice. Josh recounts being praised for German in Germany and a bonding moment with a local in a Munich beer garden.

segments.title: English accent spread, rhotic history and received pronunciation
segments.summary: English spread to Australia, India, Canada and the US with distinct accents. Australian English formed from mixed English regional accents. Rhotic and non-rhotic speech history is covered, with early American settlers sounding more like southeastern England. Received pronunciation developed as an aspirational accent and was cemented by BBC broadcasts in the 1920s.

segments.title: Accent myths, Chuck Yeager, and mid-Atlantic movie speech
segments.summary: Claims that isolated Appalachian or Outer Banks pockets preserve colonial accents have been debunked. Chuck Yeager's Appalachian accent is said to have influenced pilots' radio speech. Hollywood's mid-Atlantic accent spread via dialect coaching and popular stars, and Nancy Elliott's study showed declining r-dropping in American film actors.

segments.title: Accent perception, bias and movie accent stereotypes
segments.summary: Accents are in-group markers, and studies find people distrust foreign accents. Movie villains often have British accents, which is discussed in terms of cultural cringe. Josh and Chuck also discuss a John Hodgeman audition coached for a Southern accent.

segments.title: Accents in singing, UK grime and UK accent discrimination
segments.summary: Pop singers often sound American regardless of origin, due to pop music accent and melody. UK grime is a heavily accented rap genre. UK workplace accent discrimination is reported, citing a Guardian article about a survey.

segments.title: Movie accents: The Limey and actor accent breakdowns
segments.summary: Discussion of Terence Stamp's Cockney accent in The Limey and a video breakdown of thirty-two movie accents, including Kevin Costner's Robin Hood and Ewan McGregor's Scottish accent.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nick from Indiana
segments.summary: Nick says he had pictured the hosts backwards with each voice until he watched a video of them, which was jarring.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminders for contact channels and the website.
